No t e
Recall Hickman and Thomson’s point that “[o]nce an agency has publicly 
staked out a position and given effect to that position [by imposing an IFR],” it 
is possible that “forces like regulatory inertia, status quo bias, confirmation 
bias, and commitment bias aU make it less likely the agency will deviate from 
its position”—and, further, that “citizens might not take seriously the 
opportunity to offer comments after a rule is in effect, believing that, because 
an agency has already committed to enforcing a particular rule, submitting 
comments would just be a waste of time.” These potential problems with IFRs 
were not at their full intensity in the Little Sisters litigation, because the 
challengers obtained a preliminary injunction against the 2017 IFRs soon after 
they were issued, meaning they remained ineffective from that point until the 
Supreme Court decided the case. When the public was commenting in 
contemplation of the final rules, it did not have to live under the IFRs. Perhaps 
the case would have looked different to the Justices had this been otherwise. 
In any event, decisions on whether to grant preliminary relief have especially 
high stakes when it comes to IFRs. Little Sisters suggests the agency may be 
able to moot many or all procedural problems with an IFR once it completes 
notice and comment and promulgates a final rule.
w Because we conclude that the IFRs’ request for comment satisfies the APA’s rulemaking 
requirements, we need not reach respondents’ additional argument that the Departments lacked 
good cause to promulgate the 2017 IFRs.
